question.text:
Which of the following is MOST LIKELY to result in a whole-lung ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch on a ventilation-perfusion lung scan?
Answer Choices: (A) Foreign body in a mainstem bronchus (B) Pulmonary arterial compression by tumor (C) Large pleural effusion (D) Mucous plugging (E) Chronic thromboembolic disease (F) Superior vena cava syndrome (G) Fibrosing mediastinitis (H) Unilateral pulmonary artery hypoplasia (I) Mediastinal fibrosis from histoplasmosis (J) Extrinsic vascular compression by lymphadenopathy

options.A: Foreign body in a mainstem bronchus

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: A V/Q mismatch occurs when ventilation and perfusion are not matched in the lungs. A foreign body in a mainstem bronchus will cause ventilation to one lung while the other lung is relatively unaffected, leading to a significant V/Q mismatch. The other options are less likely to cause a whole-lung V/Q mismatch.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: A foreign body in a mainstem bronchus will cause ventilation to one lung while the other lung is relatively unaffected, leading to a significant V/Q mismatch.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Pulmonary arterial compression by tumor (B) and Extrinsic vascular compression by lymphadenopathy (J) can cause V/Q mismatch, but typically not a whole-lung mismatch. Large pleural effusion (C) and Mucous plugging (D) can cause localized V/Q mismatch, but not a whole-lung mismatch. Chronic thromboembolic disease (E) and Superior vena cava syndrome (F) can cause V/Q mismatch, but typically not a whole-lung mismatch. Fibrosing mediastinitis (G) and Unilateral pulmonary artery hypoplasia (H) are less likely to cause a whole-lung V/Q mismatch.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: Pulmonary arterial compression by tumor directly affects blood flow to a portion of the lung, creating a ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Tumor compression reduces perfusion while ventilation remains normal, leading to a V/Q mismatch. This is the most direct cause among the options.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Direct compression of pulmonary arteries by tumor
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: While other options like foreign body or pleural effusion can cause V/Q mismatch, they primarily affect ventilation or both V/Q. Tumor compression specifically targets perfusion, making it the most likely cause.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: A foreign body in a mainstem bronchus causes complete obstruction of airflow to the affected lung, leading to absent ventilation while perfusion may still occur (due to collateral circulation or delayed washout), resulting in a classic 'whole-lung' V/Q mismatch. Other options cause partial or regional mismatch, not whole-lung.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Complete bronchial obstruction leads to absent ventilation in the entire affected lung while perfusion may persist, creating a whole-lung V/Q mismatch.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Chronic thromboembolic disease (E) and pulmonary arterial compression (B) cause regional perfusion defects, not whole-lung mismatch. Large pleural effusion (C) and mucous plugging (D) cause partial ventilation/perfusion defects. Superior vena cava syndrome (F) and mediastinal fibrosis (G, I) may cause bilateral or regional effects, not whole-lung. Extrinsic compression (J) and hypoplasia (H) are less likely to cause complete unilateral mismatch.

olmo3_7b.clinical_reasoning: A large pleural effusion most likely causes a reduction in lung expansion, leading to areas of low alveolar volume and thus ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch even if perfusion is normal in those regions. Other options like foreign body, tumor compression, fibrosis, or congenital hypoplasia may cause V/Q mismatch but are less directly associated with the pattern seen in a typical ventilation-perfusion scan result compared to pleural effusion, which is well-known to produce patchy or lobe-level perfusion defects without corresponding ventilation changes in the same areas.
olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: Large pleural effusion reduces lung expansion, decreasing ventilation in the affected lung regions while perfusion remains relatively normal, creating V/Q mismatch.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Options such as foreign body (A), tumor compression (B), and fibrotic lesions (G, I) can cause V/Q mismatch but are more likely to result in absolute or relative perfusion defects with varying ventilation involvement. Unilateral pulmonary artery hypoplasia (H) and extrinsic vascular compression (J) might affect perfusion but are less common causes of the specific V/Q mismatch pattern seen in a pleural effusion. Mucous plugging (D) and chronic thromboembolic disease (E) cause perfusion defects but not the same V/Q mismatch mechanism as pleural effusion.
